title: Collecting pupil voice about classroom talk fd1fcbb6cc78bfc1c0065e5ed5f39389dfc63866a0c7a926895036d9c
author: Oracy Cambridge
source: Oracy Cambridge newsletter (Hughes Hall, University of Cambridge), October 9, 2026
summary: This installment of the Oracy Cambridge email series, written by Topsy for oracy leads and teachers, argues that finding out what students think is a vital way to monitor the impact of oracy work. It offers ten ready-to-use questions that probe whether students know what oracy is, who does most of the talking, how participation is decided, how well peers listen, and what teachers could do better. The second half gives practical advice for running the conversations: keep groups to four to six, check the sample is representative, rephrase questions so they are not leading, and ask every student to answer every question. It also stresses careful listening, noting exact student words, and following up on surprising answers. The piece closes by insisting that leaders act on what they hear by sharing findings with colleagues and agreeing priorities, and it ends with a pointer to a listening observation tool and the Implementing Oracy 2027 programme.
points: Ten student-facing questions, from 'Can talking help with learning?' to 'Who does most of the talking?', give a quick audit of classroom talk practices that does not depend on lesson observation alone.
Sampling matters: small groups of four to six that are representative of the cohort keep the pupil voice from being dominated by the most confident students.
Question phrasing is a design choice, so replacing 'Do you like talk partners?' with 'Talk partners: are they a good idea or a bad idea?' avoids leading answers.
Asking each student to respond to each question, and to react to what a classmate said, draws out a wider range of perspectives than open discussion.
Pupil voice only counts as impact monitoring if it is acted on, so record exact words and bring findings to team meetings to decide priorities.
quotes: One thing that you’ll want to do as an oracy lead, or teacher who is implementing oracy, is to find out what your students think. This is a vital way of monitoring impact.
Here are ten questions you might like to ask students. Their responses will give you an insight into classroom talk practices in your school.
Groupings: Consider which students are being selected. Are they representative of the cohort? Keep groups small – four-six.
Phrasing: You may need to rephrase some questions so that everyone understands what you’re asking. Be careful not to make the questions ‘leading’.
Be interested: Encourage students to speak freely and let them know that you are genuinely interested in what they think.
We often have ideas or hopes around what they’ll say, but we need to be open. If they say something surprising, ask for more detail so you can understand
Action: Do something with your findings. For example, share with colleagues, discuss at team meetings etc.
